name: Global Monopole and Letelier's Cloud of Strings
description: The static, spherically symmetric field of a global monopole, a hedgehog of three scalar fields that forms where a global O(3) symmetry breaks, and of Letelier's cloud of strings running out from a centre. Every sphere about the centre misses the same fraction of its solid angle, so light passing it is bent through one angle whatever its impact parameter, and with a mass at the centre it holds a black hole.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit. The deficit $\Delta$ is dimensionless and $r_s$ a length. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: A universe cooling through a phase transition can leave defects behind where its symmetry breaks, and Tom Kibble showed in 1976 that whether they are domain walls, strings, or monopoles depends on the homotopy groups of the manifold of degenerate vacua [kibble1976]. A global monopole forms where a global $O(3)$ symmetry of a triplet of scalar fields breaks; its field is a hedgehog, the triplet pointing straight out from the core in every direction [barriola1989, guendelman1991]. The monopole's mass grows linearly with the distance from its core [harari1990].¶Patricio Letelier gave in 1979 a gauge invariant form of the model of a cloud of strings that John Stachel was developing, studied its energy conditions, and solved Einstein's equations for such a cloud with spherical symmetry, with plane symmetry, and in one case of cylindrical symmetry [letelier1979, stachel1980]. Letelier's spherical cloud surrounds a mass $m$ at its centre, with the line element $ds^2 = -(1 - a - 2m/r)dt^2 + dr^2/(1 - a - 2m/r) + r^2d\Omega^2$, a constant $a$ setting the density of strings, and a horizon at $r = 2m/(1 - a)$ [letelier1979]. He used the solution to build a model of a star in two layers [letelier1979].¶Manuel Barriola and Alexander Vilenkin found in 1989 the field outside a global monopole, an approximate solution of Einstein's equations [barriola1989]. Far from the core it is Letelier's metric, with $a = 8\pi G\eta^2$ for the symmetry breaking scale $\eta$ and a small mass at the origin [barriola1989, harari1990]. The monopole exerts practically no gravitational force on slow matter, the space around it has a deficit solid angle, and every light ray passing it is deflected by the same angle, whatever its impact parameter [barriola1989]. With the mass dropped and $t$ and $r$ rescaled by $\sqrt{1 - \Delta}$, $\Delta = 8\pi G\eta^2$, a sphere at the proper distance $r$ from the centre has the area $4\pi(1 - \Delta)r^2$, short of Euclid's by the solid angle $4\pi\Delta$ [barriola1989]. Vilenkin's cosmic string removes a wedge from every plane through it, and the monopole removes a solid angle from every sphere around it [vilenkin1981, barriola1989]. Eduardo Guendelman and A. Rabinowitz showed in 1991 that the same gravitational field comes from cosmic strings crossing at one point, in the limit of a continuous distribution of them over every direction, which they called the string hedgehog [guendelman1991].¶The small mass is negative, as Diego Harari and Carlos Lousto showed in 1990 [harari1990]. A global monopole therefore repels matter, as domain walls and global strings do [harari1990]. They solved the coupled equations of the metric and the scalar field numerically, to fix that repulsive potential and to follow the solution where gravity is already strong near the core, and they followed test particles moving around the monopole [harari1990].¶Guendelman and Rabinowitz also found that the geometry is static only while the hedgehog's energy density is small, and for larger densities is an anisotropic cosmology [guendelman1991]. Alexander Vilenkin showed in 1994 that inflation can take place in the core of a topological defect, where the scalar field is held near the maximum of its potential, with no fine tuning of the initial conditions [vilenkin1994]. Andrei Linde showed the same year that monopoles formed during new inflation expand exponentially and go on inflating after inflation has ended around them [linde1994]. Dieter Maison and Steven Liebling derived in 1999 the largest scale of a static monopole exactly, $\eta_{max} = \sqrt{3/8\pi}$ with $G = 1$, which is $\Delta = 3$, where the static monopole bifurcates with the de Sitter solution of a vanishing Higgs field [maison1999]. Liebling found in 2000 static monopoles with no horizon for $\Delta < 1$, apparently regular ones with a horizon for $1 \le \Delta \lesssim 3$, and none beyond, consistent with topological inflation setting in near $\eta = 0.33$ with $G = 1$ [liebling2000].¶David Bennett and Sun Hong Rhie simulated global monopoles in an expanding universe in 1990 and found them settling into a scaling solution, a fixed number in every horizon volume, so that monopoles formed at the grand unification scale could seed galaxies and large scale structure [bennett1990]. Ue-Li Pen, David Spergel, and Neil Turok simulated textures, global monopoles, and global strings and found each consistent with the microwave anisotropy detected by the Cosmic Background Explorer, for a high bias factor [pen1994]. With Uroš Seljak, Pen and Turok computed the power spectra of those models more precisely in 1997 and found vector modes carrying about half the anisotropy on large scales, which suppressed the acoustic peaks and left the matter fluctuations a factor of five below those of inflation [pen1997]. In their words, "Current observations of CMB anisotropies and galaxy clustering do not favor the models under consideration" [pen1997].

related.text: The monopole unwound, $\Delta = 0$, with every sphere whole again.
The defect along a line. It removes a wedge from every plane it crosses, where the monopole removes a solid angle from every sphere [vilenkin1981, barriola1989].
The defect spread over a surface. A wall repels matter, as a global monopole does [kibble1976, harari1990].

coordinates.name: Static Spherical

parameters.description: Solid angle deficit, the fraction of $4\pi$ missing from every sphere about the centre, $0 \le \Delta < 1$: $8\pi G\eta^2$ in units with $\hbar = c = 1$ for a global monopole of symmetry breaking scale $\eta$, and Letelier's $a$ for a cloud of strings

Schwarzschild radius of the mass at the centre, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with its horizon at $r_h = r_s/(1 - \Delta)$: positive for a black hole in a cloud of strings, negative and small outside a global monopole's core

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Barriola-Vilenkin

parameters.description: Solid angle deficit, the fraction of $4\pi$ missing from every sphere about the centre, $0 \le \Delta < 1$: $8\pi G\eta^2$ in units with $\hbar = c = 1$ for a global monopole of symmetry breaking scale $\eta$, and Letelier's $a$ for a cloud of strings

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the proper distance from the centre, with no mass at the centre, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Solid angle deficit, the fraction of $4\pi$ missing from every sphere about the centre, $0 \le \Delta < 1$: $8\pi G\eta^2$ in units with $\hbar = c = 1$ for a global monopole of symmetry breaking scale $\eta$, and Letelier's $a$ for a cloud of strings

Schwarzschild radius of the mass at the centre, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with its horizon at $r_h = r_s/(1 - \Delta)$: positive for a black hole in a cloud of strings, negative and small outside a global monopole's core

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded time $u = ct - r_*$ a length, where $r_* = r/(1 - \Delta) + r_s\ln\left|(1 - \Delta)r/r_s - 1\right|/(1 - \Delta)^2$.

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Solid angle deficit, the fraction of $4\pi$ missing from every sphere about the centre, $0 \le \Delta < 1$: $8\pi G\eta^2$ in units with $\hbar = c = 1$ for a global monopole of symmetry breaking scale $\eta$, and Letelier's $a$ for a cloud of strings

Schwarzschild radius of the mass at the centre, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with its horizon at $r_h = r_s/(1 - \Delta)$: positive for a black hole in a cloud of strings, negative and small outside a global monopole's core

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v = ct + r_*$ a length, where $r_* = r/(1 - \Delta) + r_s\ln\left|(1 - \Delta)r/r_s - 1\right|/(1 - \Delta)^2$.
